title: An Examination of Generative AI Response to Suicide Inquires: Content Analysis
study_design: Longitudinal content analysis conducted in two phases (spring 2023 and summer 2024) of general-purpose generative AI chatbot responses to suicide-related prompts, supplemented by LIWC-22 linguistic analysis
population: General-purpose generative AI chatbots responding to suicide-related prompts framed as youth/adolescent-style inquiries about a suicidal friend
sample_size: Phase 1: 3 chatbots analyzed (ChatGPT 3.5, Bing Chat, Google Bard); Phase 2: 7 chatbots analyzed (ChatGPT 3.5, Microsoft CoPilot, Google Gemini, Claude 2, xAI Grok 2, Mistral AI, Meta AI)
country_or_setting: United States; web-based chatbot platforms queried by researchers
ai_type_application: Large language model generative AI chatbots used for mental health/suicide information and crisis-support responses
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to chatbot-generated responses to 5 suicide-related prompts in phase 1 and 7 prompts in phase 2, designed to simulate adolescent help-seeking about a suicidal friend
comparator_control_group: No formal control group; comparisons were across chatbot platforms and across two time points (phase 1 vs phase 2)
mental_health_outcome: Quality, accuracy, empathy, tone, authenticity, mention of crisis resources, lethality assessment, supportive guidance, and potentially harmful content in AI responses about suicide
outcome_measurement_tool: Human-coded content analysis and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC-22) for authenticity and emotional tone
positive_effects: Responses became more comprehensive and responsive from phase 1 to phase 2; more chatbots provided suicide hotline information including 988; phase 2 responses more often included resources, urgency, support, nonjudgmental language, attention to lethality, normalization of outreach, care for the reporter, and alternatives to suicide
negative_effects_harms: In phase 1, resources were scant and lethality was not addressed. Microsoft CoPilot in phase 2 sometimes attempted to change the subject and forced the user to restart the conversation. One chatbot provided an unsolicited image depicting suicide, which authors note could be triggering or a risk factor for someone in crisis. The paper also discusses external examples of harmful chatbot interactions, but these were not part of this study's own data.
evidence_type: Observational descriptive evidence from chatbot output analysis; not human participant outcome data
main_finding: General generative AI chatbots showed improved suicide-related responses over one year, with greater depth, accuracy, empathy, and referral to crisis resources in phase 2, but important safety concerns remained, including inconsistent handling and one unsolicited suicide image.
effect_size_key_result: No inferential effect size reported. LIWC examples: ChatGPT 3.5 word count increased from 500 to 2198 and authenticity from 27.35 to 60.03 between phases; Google Bard/Gemini had the highest emotional tone scores (76.54 in phase 1; 79.99 in phase 2); Microsoft Bing/CoPilot had the lowest tone scores (37.99 in phase 1; 32.09 in phase 2).
limitations_bias: No human participants or direct mental health outcomes were measured; only free chatbot accounts were used; chatbot models and outputs change over time; prompts concerned a suicidal friend rather than self-disclosure; some platform access differed by time and account; coding involved researcher interpretation; results may not generalize to paid versions or future model iterations.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as evidence about potential effects of AI-delivered mental health information quality and safety in suicide-related contexts, but it does not measure mental health outcomes in users. Best suited as contextual or harms/safety evidence rather than effect-on-mental-health efficacy evidence.
reason_for_decision: The paper directly concerns AI in a mental health context and reports potential harms and supportive features, but it does not assess effects of AI on human mental health outcomes. Inclusion depends on whether the review includes safety/content studies in addition to outcome studies.
notes_for_research_question: This study is useful for a systematic review section on safety, crisis communication quality, and possible adverse effects of general-purpose AI chatbots in mental health contexts, especially suicide-related inquiries. It does not provide participant-level evidence that AI improved or worsened mental health.
